questions.question: In the dengue classification experiment, the model achieved a training accuracy of 0.9732 and a testing accuracy of 0.9740. What does this indicate about the model?

answers.a: The model is severely overfitting the training data
answers.b: The model generalises well since training and testing accuracies are very close
answers.c: The model is underfitting and needs more features
answers.d: The testing accuracy should always be much lower than training accuracy

explanations.a: Overfitting is characterised by a significant gap where training accuracy is much higher than testing accuracy, which is not the case here.
explanations.b: When training and testing accuracies are nearly equal and both high, the model has learnt the underlying pattern without memorising noise.
explanations.c: Underfitting would lead to poor performance on both training and testing sets, which contradicts the high values observed.
explanations.d: There is no rule requiring testing accuracy to be much lower; a well-trained model should show similar performance on both sets.

questions.question: The confusion matrix for the testing data shows some false negatives (dengue-positive patients classified as negative). In a medical diagnosis context, why is minimising false negatives critical?

answers.a: False negatives reduce the precision of the model
answers.b: False negatives increase the specificity of the model
answers.c: A false negative means a sick patient is incorrectly cleared, potentially delaying life-saving treatment
answers.d: False negatives only affect the ROC curve and have no clinical significance

explanations.a: False negatives affect recall (sensitivity), not precision. Precision is affected by false positives.
explanations.b: Specificity is computed from true negatives and false positives; false negatives do not appear in the specificity formula.
explanations.c: In medical diagnosis, failing to detect a disease (false negative) can lead to untreated illness and serious consequences for the patient.
explanations.d: False negatives have direct clinical implications beyond their effect on any performance curve.

questions.question: The F1-Score is defined as 2TP2TP + FP + FN. When is the F1-Score a more appropriate evaluation metric than accuracy?

answers.a: When the dataset has perfectly balanced classes
answers.b: When the dataset has imbalanced class distributions
answers.d: When the model outputs continuous values

explanations.a: With balanced classes, accuracy and F1-Score generally convey similar information.
explanations.b: In imbalanced datasets, accuracy can be misleadingly high if the model predicts the majority class. F1-Score accounts for both precision and recall, providing a more meaningful measure.
explanations.c: F1-Score does not include true negatives in its formula; it focuses on the positive class.
explanations.d: F1-Score is computed after thresholding probabilities into discrete class labels, not on continuous outputs.

questions.question: In the simulation, the ROC curve was plotted with AUC = 0.998. What does an AUC value close to 1.0 signify?

answers.a: The model performs no better than random guessing
answers.b: The model has near-perfect ability to distinguish between dengue-positive and dengue-negative patients across all thresholds
answers.c: The model always predicts the majority class
answers.d: The model has high bias and low variance

explanations.a: Random guessing produces an AUC of approximately 0.5, not close to 1.0.
explanations.b: An AUC near 1.0 means that for virtually every threshold, the true positive rate is high while the false positive rate remains low, indicating excellent discriminative capability.
explanations.c: Predicting only the majority class would yield a single point on the ROC plot, not a curve with AUC near 1.
explanations.d: High bias (underfitting) would produce a low AUC, not a value near 1.

questions.question: During the simulation, individual sigmoid curves were plotted for features like Platelets and Hematocrit. If the sigmoid curve for a feature shows a steep transition from 0 to 1, what can be inferred?

answers.a: The feature has no discriminative power for dengue classification
answers.b: The feature values overlap completely between the two classes
answers.c: The feature strongly separates the two classes, and the model assigns high confidence near the transition region
answers.d: The model is underfitting that particular feature

explanations.a: A non-discriminative feature would produce a nearly flat sigmoid with little transition, not a steep one.
explanations.b: Complete overlap would prevent the sigmoid from showing a clear transition region.
explanations.c: A steep sigmoid indicates that a small change in the feature value leads to a large change in predicted probability, implying strong class separation.
explanations.d: Underfitting would manifest as poor overall performance, not as a steep sigmoid for one feature.

questions.question: In the experiment, precision on the test set was 0.9657 and recall was 0.9783. If the application requires minimising false positives (e.g., avoiding unnecessary treatments), which metric should be prioritised?

answers.a: Recall, because it captures all positive cases
answers.b: Precision, because it measures the proportion of predicted positives that are truly positive
answers.c: Accuracy, because it reflects overall correctness
answers.d: Specificity, because it measures the true negative rate

explanations.a: Recall focuses on minimising false negatives, not false positives.
explanations.b: Precision = TPTP + FP. A high precision means that when the model predicts positive, it is very likely correct, thereby reducing unnecessary treatments.
explanations.c: Accuracy does not distinguish between types of errors and may not reflect the cost of false positives.
explanations.d: Specificity = TNTN + FP which is related but precision more directly addresses the concern about predicted positives.

questions.question: In the simulation, the dataset was split into 80% training and 20% testing with stratified sampling. What is the purpose of stratified splitting?

answers.a: To ensure that both training and testing sets have the same proportion of dengue-positive and dengue-negative cases
answers.b: To randomly shuffle the data without preserving class ratios
answers.c: To allocate all positive cases to the training set
answers.d: To increase the size of the testing set

explanations.a: Stratified splitting preserves the original class distribution in both subsets, preventing training or testing bias due to unequal class representation.
explanations.b: Random splitting without stratification does not guarantee that class proportions are maintained.
explanations.c: Allocating all positive cases to training would leave no positive examples for testing, making evaluation impossible.
explanations.d: Stratification controls class ratios, not the overall size of the splits.

questions.question: The logistic regression model in the experiment used L2 regularization with C = 1.0. If C is decreased to 0.01, what is the expected effect?

answers.a: Stronger regularization, leading to smaller weight coefficients and potentially higher bias
answers.b: Weaker regularization, allowing larger weights and potentially higher variance
answers.c: No change, since C does not affect the model
answers.d: The model will switch from classification to regression

explanations.a: In scikit-learn, C is the inverse of regularization strength. A smaller C means stronger regularization, which penalises large weights more heavily, shrinking coefficients and possibly increasing bias.
explanations.b: Decreasing C increases regularization strength, not decreases it.
explanations.c: C directly controls the trade-off between fitting the data and keeping weights small.
explanations.d: Changing C does not alter the nature of the algorithm; logistic regression remains a classifier.

questions.question: If the ROC curve is plotted for the dengue classification model and the curve passes through the point (FPR = 0.05, TPR = 0.95), what does this specific operating point represent?

answers.a: The model misclassifies 95% of negative cases and correctly identifies 5% of positive cases
answers.b: At this threshold, 95% of actual dengue-positive patients are detected while only 5% of dengue-negative patients are incorrectly flagged as positive
answers.c: The model has 95% precision and 5% recall
answers.d: The total error rate of the model is 5%

explanations.a: FPR = 0.05 means only 5% of negatives are misclassified, not 95%.
explanations.b: TPR (sensitivity) of 0.95 means 95% of positives are correctly detected; FPR of 0.05 means only 5% of negatives are falsely classified as positive.
explanations.c: The ROC curve plots TPR against FPR, not precision against recall.
explanations.d: The total error rate depends on the class distribution and both types of errors, not just the FPR.

questions.question: In the experiment, the Platelets feature was dropped before training. If a highly correlated but less clinically relevant feature is kept instead, what issue might arise in the model coefficients?

answers.a: The coefficients become uninterpretable due to multicollinearity, though predictions may still be accurate
answers.b: The model automatically removes correlated features
answers.c: The sigmoid function changes its shape
answers.d: The model will produce an AUC of exactly 0.5

explanations.a: Multicollinearity inflates the variance of coefficient estimates, making individual weight interpretation unreliable, even though the overall predictive performance may remain stable.
explanations.b: Standard logistic regression does not perform automatic feature selection; L1 regularization can push some coefficients to zero but L2 does not.
explanations.c: The sigmoid function transforms the linear combination; its mathematical form does not change due to feature correlation.
explanations.d: Multicollinearity affects coefficient stability, not the discriminative ability to the extent of reducing AUC to 0.5.
